The short version: the book's material on making your own chroma keyer is rich and opinionated, but the retrieved evidence contains **nothing about nonsquare pixels** — that topic is absent from what I can ground the comparison in, so the two-sided comparison can't be completed on the corpus.

## What the book says about making your own chroma keyer

The DIY recipe starts by converting the RGB image to HSV, then piping it through a color curve: the red curve now holds Hue data, green holds Saturation, and blue holds Value (brightness), so you adjust the three curves to include or exclude the hue, saturation, and value ranges of the target object [S1]. The underlying principle is that the keyer works in HSV/HSL internally rather than RGB, because saturation isn't an RGB attribute — a starting pixel defines the "center" of the key, ranges are set for H, S, and V, pixels inside the ranges go white and those outside go black, and tolerances on each setting produce the soft edges [S13]. A more flexible twist described in the book is a homemade 3D color keyer that works on arbitrary colors via a simplified version of Primatte's principles, operating in the RGB color-cube space [S7].

The book's verdict on the DIY approach is notably skeptical: unlike the luma keyer, where cleverness can meaningfully beat the basic version, a homemade chroma keyer "will probably be more hassle than it's worth" — worth attempting once to test your mettle, but an off-the-shelf chroma keyer is hard to improve upon [S2]. That skepticism sits in a broader context where the book stresses that a chroma key is specifically a hue-and-saturation-based extraction from HSV/HSL data, whereas most greenscreen tools are actually color difference keyers like Keylight, Ultimatte, or Fusion's Delta Keyer [S4][S6], and where its advice is to try a chroma key first for speed, then break out a color difference key for nicer edges [S15].

There is no retrieved material on nonsquare pixels at all. The evidence covers chroma key theory, DIY keyer construction, the 3D variant, and commercial keyers, but never touches pixel geometry. So the specific fact needed for the comparison — what this book says about nonsquare pixels, their causes, and their correction — is missing, and I won't reconstruct the book's position from general knowledge. results.question: Compare what the book says about miscellaneous drawing tips with what it says about transc
results.answer:
The corpus handles the two halves of this question very unevenly. The miscellaneous drawing tips — documented mostly in Francis Glebas's *Directing the Story* and echoed by the manga and life-drawing books — are richly covered; transcoding versus color rerendering appears nowhere in the retrieved material. The requested comparison therefore has a firm first half and an evidence-free second half.

## What the drawing tips actually say

The tips cluster around four concerns. **Legibility:** a drawing should survive the blacken-in test — fill in the values and the action must still read; keep decoration inside the main outline; draw bold with a grease pencil, marker, or 2B so the marks read from across the room; stick to one idea per sketch; and number your drawings [S1][S2][S3]. **Design interest:** avoid symmetry, use angles instead of rigid poses, play straight lines against curves, give outlines real character, and compose to drawn borders [S1][S3][S6]. **Expressiveness:** feel the pose kinetically in your own body, show how the character feels, remember a person is always "doing" something, darken pupils, and use straight-line symbols for stretches and bent lines for squashes [S3][S6]. **Process:** don't be afraid to redraw, cut out parts that don't work and rework them, start from a rough sketch that clarifies the final image, and balance technique (perspective, anatomy, force, shape) against honest observation [S3][S5][S9].

Practically, these tips share one goal: an image that communicates its story instantly and unambiguously, even from a distance, without decorative clutter. That is why the books warn against "clever" camera angles that produce ambiguity and insist everything in a sketch be subordinated to its single important idea [S6].

## The missing half

None of the retrieved sources discusses transcoding or color rerendering, so nothing in the corpus can be compared on that side — the premise is simply absent. In general color-science usage (beyond what these sources cover), transcoding means converting encoded image data between formats or color spaces while preserving numeric values, whereas color rendering/rerendering aims to reproduce the *appearance* of colors for a different display or viewing condition; but no sentence in this corpus addresses either concept.

results.question: Compare what the book says about transcoding versus color rerendering with what it says ab
results.answer:
The short version: the corpus draws a sharp technical line between **transcoding** and **color rerendering** as two ways to move color data between displays, but it has no substantive discussion of the film *Face/Off* at all — only an index entry pointing to it, so the two topics can't actually be compared in content, only in kind.

**What the book distinguishes.** Transcoding applies when the two displays match in black level, white luminance, gamma, and viewing conditions but differ in primary chromaticities: you linearize the first display's encoded RGB, convert to CIE XYZ, convert to the second display's RGB, and re-impose its encoding nonlinearity [S2]. Color rerendering applies when contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar: you undo whatever color rendering was done for the first display, recover the non-color-rendered XYZ values, and re-render them for the second display [S1]. The background concept, per the same handbook, is that *color rendering* is the transformation of an image to account for differences in viewing environment — e.g., a still camera rendering a desert-sunlit scene into an image intended for a dimmer office monitor [S3]. Raw encodings defer this rendering downstream, while baked-in rendering in non-raw formats is hard to undo [S6].

| Aspect | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| When used | Displays match in black/white, gamma, viewing conditions; primaries differ [S2] | Contrast, whites, or viewing conditions grossly differ [S1] |
| Core operation | Linearize → XYZ → target RGB → re-encode [S2] | Undo old rendering → XYZ → render for new environment [S1] |
| What's preserved | The encoded color values via a numeric remap | Perceptual intent despite a changed viewing environment |

**What the corpus says about FACE OFF.** Only one hit exists: an index entry in *Fight Choreography: The Art of Non-Verbal Dialogue* listing "Face-Off (1997), 281, 344" [S5]. That's a page pointer to the film, with no actual discussion of it in the retrieved material, and nothing linking it to color science. One likely mix-up worth naming: the VES Handbook does have a section on **Face Paste**, but that's a facial motion-capture technique — capture done separately and pasted onto body animation — not a color process, so it's equally unrelated to transcoding or rerendering [S14].

So the honest comparison is structural: transcoding and rerendering are two calibrated strategies for display-to-display color conversion, while *Face/Off* appears only as a cited film in a fight-choreography index. The evidence doesn't show why the film is referenced on those pages, and it contains no basis to connect the movie to either color process.

The handbook treats affect, fatigue, and injury as **control states** — structured, time-varying quantities a system tracks and reacts to — rather than as static labels or simple stimulus→response cues.

results.question: Compare what the book says about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states with what
results.answer:
Both ideas rest on the same underlying claim — **movement means nothing in isolation** — but they run in opposite directions. In the handbook, affect, fatigue, and injury are described as control states that must causally drive how movement is generated and executed; in *The Visual Story*, an object's movement against its background is described as a perceptual relationship that determines what the audience actually sees as motion.

**What the book says about affect, fatigue, and injury as control states**

These states are defined operationally, as movement-facing variables with update rules, not as adjectives pasted onto finished choreography [S11]. Affect is tracked through fields like movement initiation latency, acceleration profile, posture amplitude and contraction/expansion, gaze allocation, willingness to accept unstable support, and recovery patience versus urgency [S3]; an appraisal event (goal congruence, controllability, certainty) updates valence, arousal, and dominance, and those updated values must produce behavioral effects — narrower attention toward an exit lane, more urgent but less clean recovery, higher risk tolerance for one attempt [S11]. Fatigue is two-layered: global exertion (RPE, breath cycle, recovery rate) plus per-region local capacity, whose coordination effects include step-width variability and longer stabilization after hard redirection [S12]. Injury must specify mechanical consequences (load acceptance, flexion tolerance, push-off capacity), compensations (favoring the other leg, shortening stance, trunk lean), and explicit uncertainty about the source of the annotation [S1].

The handbook's continuity metrics enforce this "control state" reading: affect-to-action coupling, fatigue propagation, and injury compensation consistency are all measured as ratios, and the declared failure states are telling — emotion that appears "only in label or face," an exertion that never changes later action, or an injured region performing at baseline [S5]. In other words, a state that doesn't alter subsequent movement is a failed state.

**What it says about movement of an object with a background**

Here the relationship is perceptual rather than causal. In the quality discussion, shot affinity works because the object moves in the same direction and along the same curve as its background, which lowers visual intensity [S2]. The more striking case is induced movement: a moving object effectively transfers its movement to a nearby stationary object, so the stationary object appears to move and the mover appears still [S6]. The related film-craft accounts agree — partially covering a moving player with foreground objects introduces motion parallax that conveys position and distance to the viewer [S14], and in compositing, if the camera moves, the background must be moved to match via match moving, or the shot breaks [S10]. In every case, what the viewer perceives as "the object's movement" cannot be read from the object alone.

**The comparison**

| Dimension | Affect / fatigue / injury | Object movement vs background |
|---|---|---|
| Kind of thing | Internal control states [S11] | Perceptual figure–ground relationship [S2] |
| Direction of influence | State → future movement (production) [S5] | Relative motion → perceived movement (reception) [S6] |
| What defines meaning | The mover's internal condition | The object's motion relative to the backdrop |
| Failure mode | Emotion only in label, injury at baseline [S5] | Object and background move alike → apparent stillness, low intensity [S2] |
| Shared principle | Movement quality cannot be appended after the fact [S11] | Movement cannot be judged from the mover alone [S2][S6] |

The deepest overlap is induced movement: a "stationary" body can read as moving purely because of what the background does — the perceptual mirror of the handbook's claim that the same motion can only be produced correctly given the mover's internal state. One account treats the state as the control variable for generating movement; the other treats the object–background relation as the control variable for perceiving it. The caveat is that these come from different works in your corpus — the handbook's control-state model versus Block's compositional theory (with Mascelli and the VES handbook supplying the staging and compositing practices) — so this is a conceptual comparison, not something the handbook itself draws.

On the movement side, the material — principally Bruce Block's *The Visual Story* — treats an object's movement as perceptible only in relation to the frame line, which acts as the visual "background" reference. Any object that moves relative to the frame line generates a track, categorized by direction, quality, scale, and speed [S2], and movement can be seen only in that frame-line relationship because the screen is two-dimensional [S4]. Two effects describe how a background participates in perceived motion: **relative movement**, where one object's motion is gauged by its changing position against a second, stationary object, and **induced movement**, where a moving object transfers its motion to a nearby stationary one so the background appears to move instead — the transfer usually landing on the smaller, brighter object [S1][S3][S14]. The strongest contrast the book offers is stillness itself: **tableau staging**, which minimizes object movement in favor of the stationary arrangement of objects in the frame [S5]. Supporting sources add the physics and timing: Newton's first law (an object at rest stays at rest until a force moves it) [S7], and the tendency to accelerate mid-movement and slow at the ends — simple harmonic motion, with animation drawings placed closer together at the extremes [S9].

results.question: Compare what the book says about sound editing with what it says about write radio sparely
results.answer:
The books agree on one doctrine — restraint is what makes sound meaningful — but they reach it from opposite directions: spare radio writing leaves silence in the script, while sound editing carves it out of recorded material after the fact.

| Aspect | Writing radio sparely (Hey Whipple) | Sound editing (film/editing books) |
|---|---|---|
| The craft | Writing the script — pure wordsmithing, "writing in its most pure form" [S14] | Post-production: splitting dialogue into tracks, removing unwanted sounds, balancing levels [S5] |
| Core restraint | Write sparely so the talent can read slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S1] | Start from the cleanest, clearest signal; degrade for effect only deliberately [S4] |
| Dialogue | Cut explanations — no "someone's at the door" after a knock [S8] | No more dialogue than absolutely necessary; replace words only for clarity [S11][S5] |
| Sound's role | Sound effects tell the story; the listener fills the blanks [S8] | Sound partners with picture, ear and eye in unison; effects build atmosphere, music carries emotion [S10][S11] |
| Time pressure | A :30 is a tent next to a :60 house, and promo tags eat the seconds [S2] | Believability is built in the rough cut, then amplified in the final phase [S11] |
| Working temperament | Rare skill, hard to find, worth gold [S14] | Tedious, behind-the-scenes labor in the cutting room's "blessed silence" [S5][S3] |

**Shared doctrine: restraint is meaning.** Both camps treat economy as a creative engine, not a limitation. The radio advice is blunt — write sparely so the delivery can be slow and quiet [S1] — and the editing advice lands on the same target: no more dialogue than necessary, with the final phase dedicated to punctuation, atmosphere, and music that translates the film's emotions [S11]. Both trust the audience: a radio spot shouldn't waste words explaining a knock at the door because the effect itself tells the story [S8], just as the editor lets effects and music carry what narration would flatten [S7]. Both also insist on clean raw material — a script spare from the start [S1], a recording edited from the strongest possible signal with any degradation controlled by choice [S4] — and both treat restraint as the guard against noise: the radio cliché list is a catalog of tired formats to avoid [S9], and every cut produces a rhythmic beat that deliberate pacing shapes [S15].

**Where they part: direction and medium.** Spare radio writing is generative and pre-production: a writer builds the whole world from words and sound effects before anything is recorded [S8][S13]. Sound editing is subtractive and corrective: it removes, balances, and layers material that already exists, taking it from rough-cut believability to final polish [S5][S11]. The deeper reason is that radio has no image to lean on — a spot exists only as long as it's playing, so sound alone must carry the entire story [S13][S8] — while film sound's defining obligation is partnership, never fighting the picture [S10]. The two arts were siblings from the start: early sound films were dismissed as "filmed plays or radio plays with pictures" [S12]. The kinship still shows — in both, disciplined words and disciplined sound are what turn material into meaning.
